#10754. Web-Ready AI Images: Formats, Sizes, and srcset Done Right

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

AI image generation has become a normal part of many web projects. However, the image a model produces is rarely the image a browser should receive. A single large PNG straight from a generator can weigh several megabytes, ignore the visitor's screen size, and slow down your Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) before the page has a chance to impress anyone.

The good news is that the fix is not complicated. If you treat the generated image as a high-quality master file and run it through a small, repeatable pipeline, you can ship images that look sharp on every device and load quickly on slow connections.

This tutorial walks through that pipeline from start to finish: generating at the right size and aspect ratio, choosing modern formats, creating responsive variants with Node.js, writing srcset and sizes correctly, and avoiding the performance mistakes that show up most often in audits.

Image generators are built to produce visually impressive results, not optimized web assets. Their output is usually a single file at one resolution, often in PNG format, and sometimes with an aspect ratio that does not match your layout.

Sending that file directly to the browser creates three problems. First, mobile visitors download far more pixels than their screens can display. Second, PNG is a poor choice for photographic images because its lossless compression produces large files. Third, without width and height information, the browser cannot reserve space for the image, which causes layout shifts as the page loads.

A web pipeline solves all three. You generate one master image, export multiple sizes in modern formats, and let the browser choose the best version for each visitor.

Optimization starts before you export anything. The most efficient pipeline begins with an image that already fits your layout.

Look at where the image will appear and note its aspect ratio at each breakpoint. A full-width hero might use 16:9 on desktop, while a blog thumbnail might use 4:3 or 1:1. Then identify the largest size the image will ever display. For a full-width hero, that could be 1920 pixels wide on large screens, or more if you support high-density displays at wide viewports.

Your master image should be at least as large as that maximum rendered width. Upscaling a small image later almost always introduces blurriness or artifacts.

Modern image-generation models can follow detailed instructions, so describe the technical requirements in your prompt, not just the subject. Specify the aspect ratio, intended display size, visual style, and any areas that need to remain clear for HTML text. The exact controls available will depend on the tool you use, so check its official documentation before building a workflow around a particular feature.

A practical web-focused prompt might read: "hero image of a modern home office at sunrise, soft natural light, calm blue and warm wood tones, clear empty space on the left third for headline text, no text or logos in the image."

That last instruction matters. Avoid baking headlines or buttons into images. Text inside an image cannot be translated, resized for accessibility, or indexed reliably, and it often becomes unreadable at small sizes. Keep text in HTML and use the image for visuals only.

Once you have a master file, decide which formats to serve. For most photographic and illustrative AI images, a combination of AVIF, WebP, and JPEG covers every modern browser while keeping file sizes small.

AVIF typically offers the strongest compression for photographic content and is supported by all major modern browsers, including Safari 16 and later. WebP is slightly less efficient but encodes faster and has near-universal support. JPEG remains a reliable fallback for older browsers and email clients.

Use PNG only when you specifically need lossless quality, such as for sharp-edged graphics or screenshots. Both AVIF and WebP support transparency, so you rarely need PNG for images with transparent backgrounds anymore.

Creating a dozen versions of every image by hand is tedious and error-prone. Instead, script the process. The Sharp documentation explains how to resize images and export them in different formats.

Then create a script that exports several widths in each format:

const widths = [480, 768, 1080, 1440, 1920];

{ ext: 'avif', format: 'avif', options: { quality: 50 } },

{ ext: 'webp', format: 'webp', options: { quality: 75 } },

{ ext: 'jpg', format: 'jpeg', options: { quality: 80, mozjpeg: true } },

for (const { ext, format, options } of formats) {

.resize({ width, withoutEnlargement: true })

Save the file as an ES module, such as build-images.mjs, and run it with Node. The withoutEnlargement option prevents sharp from upscaling the master when a target width is larger than the original.

The quality values above are reasonable starting points, not universal rules. AVIF and WebP quality scales do not map directly to JPEG quality, so compare outputs visually at the sizes your users will actually see. Smooth gradients, which are common in AI-generated skies and backgrounds, are especially prone to banding at aggressive settings.

The MDN responsive images guide explains how srcset and sizes work. The srcset attribute lists available image files and their intrinsic widths. The sizes attribute tells the browser how wide the image will be displayed in the layout. With both pieces of information, the browser can choose the smallest file that still looks sharp on the visitor's screen, including high-density displays.

Here is an example for an image inside an article column that is 720 pixels wide on larger screens and nearly full width on smaller ones:

alt="A modern home office at sunrise with a wooden desk and soft natural light"

The most common mistake is omitting sizes or leaving it at 100vw for images that are not full width. When that happens, the browser assumes the image fills the entire viewport and downloads a much larger file than necessary. Always match sizes to your actual CSS layout.

To offer AVIF and WebP with a JPEG fallback, wrap your image in a picture element. The browser checks each source in order and uses the first format it supports. See the MDN documentation for the picture element for the full syntax.

srcset="dist/hero-768.avif 768w, dist/hero-1440.avif 1440w, dist/hero-1920.avif 1920w"

srcset="dist/hero-768.webp 768w, dist/hero-1440.webp 1440w, dist/hero-1920.webp 1920w"

srcset="dist/hero-768.jpg 768w, dist/hero-1440.jpg 1440w, dist/hero-1920.jpg 1920w"

alt="A modern home office at sunrise with a wooden desk and soft natural light"

The img element is still required. It holds the fallback file, the dimensions, the alt text, and the loading attributes, while the source elements simply provide alternative formats.

If you need a different crop on mobile, such as a square version of a wide hero, add media attributes to your source elements. This technique is called art direction, and it is a good reason to generate or crop a separate master image for small screens rather than relying on CSS to hide important parts of a wide composition.

Always include width and height attributes on your img element. Modern browsers use them to calculate the image's aspect ratio and reserve the correct space before the file downloads, which helps prevent Cumulative Layout Shift. In CSS, set the image to width: 100% and height: auto so it scales responsively while keeping its proportions.

Use loading="lazy" for images below the fold, but never on your hero or other LCP image. Lazy loading your most important image delays it unnecessarily. Instead, add fetchpriority="high" to the LCP image so the browser downloads it early.

Write alt text that describes the image's purpose in context. If an image is purely decorative, use an empty alt attribute so screen readers skip it. Generated images do not come with meaningful descriptions, so this step always requires human judgment.

Use descriptive file names, such as home-office-sunrise-1440.avif, instead of generic names like image-final-v3.png. Clear names make assets easier to manage and give search engines a small amount of extra context.

Be aware of metadata. Some AI image providers, including OpenAI, embed C2PA provenance data that identifies an image as AI-generated. sharp strips most metadata by default, which reduces file size but also removes that provenance information. If transparency matters to your project or your client, recent versions of sharp offer a keepMetadata() method, and you can also disclose AI-generated imagery in captions or credits.

In Chrome DevTools, open the Network panel, filter by images, and resize the viewport or switch to device emulation. Reload the page and confirm that smaller files load on smaller screens. You can also select the image in the Elements panel and check its currentSrc property in the console to see which file the browser actually chose.

Then run Lighthouse or PageSpeed Insights. Look for warnings about properly sized images, modern image formats, and LCP.

Not always. AVIF often produces smaller files for photographic content, but it encodes more slowly. Serving both with a JPEG fallback is a safe default.

Four to six widths usually cover most layouts. Choose them based on your breakpoints and the largest rendered size of each image.

Review the current terms of service for the model and the platform you use. Licensing terms can differ between providers and plans.

AI image generation removes much of the cost and time of creating custom visuals, but it does not remove the need for good web engineering. Generate a high-quality master at the right aspect ratio, export responsive variants in modern formats, write accurate srcset and sizes values, protect your LCP and layout stability, and test everything before you ship.

Once the pipeline is scripted, every new image takes seconds to optimize. That combination gives you the creative speed of AI and the performance your visitors expect.

#10751. AI-powered robot learns how to harvest tomatoes more efficiently

Farm labor shortages are pushing agriculture toward greater automation, especially when it comes to harvesting. But not all crops are easy for machines to handle. Tomatoes, for example, grow in clusters, which means a robot must carefully select ripe fruit while leaving unripe ones untouched. This requires precise control and smart decision-making.

To tackle this challenge, Assistant Professor Takuya Fujinaga of Osaka Metropolitan University's Graduate School of Engineering developed a system that trains robots to assess how easy each tomato is to harvest before attempting to pick it.

His approach combines image recognition with statistical analysis to determine the best angle for picking each fruit. The robot analyzes visual details such as the tomato itself, its stems, and whether it is hidden behind leaves or other parts of the plant. These inputs guide the robot in choosing the most effective way to approach and pick the fruit.

From Detection to "Harvest-Ease" Decision-Making

This method shifts away from traditional systems that focus only on detecting and identifying fruit. Instead, Fujinaga introduces what he calls "harvest-ease estimation." "This moves beyond simply asking 'can a robot pick a tomato?' to thinking about 'how likely is a successful pick?', which is more meaningful for real-world farming," he explained.

In testing, the system achieved an 81% success rate, exceeding expectations. About one-quarter of the successful picks came from tomatoes that were harvested from the side after an initial front-facing attempt failed. This indicates the robot can adjust its approach when the first attempt is not successful.

The research underscores how many variables affect robotic harvesting, including how tomatoes cluster, the shape and position of stems, surrounding leaves, and visual obstruction. "This research establishes 'ease of harvesting' as a quantitatively evaluable metric, bringing us one step closer to the realization of agricultural robots that can make informed decisions and act intelligently," Fujinaga said.

Future of Human-Robot Collaboration in Farming

Looking ahead, Fujinaga envisions robots that can independently judge when crops are ready to be picked. "This is expected to usher in a new form of agriculture where robots and humans collaborate," he explained. "Robots will automatically harvest tomatoes that are easy to pick, while humans will handle the more challenging fruits."

The findings were published in Smart Agricultural Technology.

#10747. DNA robots could deliver drugs and hunt viruses inside your body

Imagine tiny robots made from DNA moving through the bloodstream, delivering drugs exactly where they are needed and targeting threats such as cancer cells or viruses. These microscopic machines could also assemble ultra-precise data storage systems and computing devices at the nanometer scale. Although the possibilities are remarkable, most DNA robots today remain in early experimental stages and are better understood as proof of concept rather than practical tools.

Researchers are exploring how DNA can be engineered into working machines using creative design approaches. These include building rigid DNA joints, incorporating flexible components, and using folding techniques inspired by origami. By applying principles from larger-scale robotics such as rigid, compliant and origami robots, scientists are adapting familiar mechanical concepts to the nanoscale. This allows DNA-based systems to carry out controlled and repeatable tasks despite their extremely small size.

Guiding the motion of DNA robots in a constantly shifting molecular environment is a major challenge. To address this, scientists have developed control systems that help these machines behave in predictable ways. One important method involves DNA strand displacement, a biochemical process that enables precise programming of movement using specific DNA sequences labeled as "fuel" and "structure."

In addition to biochemical control, external physical signals such as electric fields, magnetic fields, and light can direct how these robots move. Together, these approaches provide a toolkit for fine-tuning the behavior of DNA machines with a high degree of accuracy.

The potential uses for DNA robots extend well beyond laboratory experiments. In medicine, they could function as "nano-surgeons," locating diseased cells and delivering targeted treatments with precision. Researchers are also exploring whether these machines could capture viruses like SARS-CoV-2, with future systems potentially operating as fully autonomous drug delivery platforms.

DNA robots may also play a role in advanced manufacturing. Acting as programmable templates, they could position nanoparticles with sub-nanometer accuracy. This capability could lead to breakthroughs in molecular computing and highly efficient optical devices that outperform current technologies.

Despite rapid progress, several obstacles remain. Moving from large-scale systems to molecular machines introduces challenges such as Brownian motion, which makes precise control more difficult. Many current DNA robot designs are still relatively simple and operate in isolation, limiting their usefulness in complex real-world environments.

There are also gaps in foundational knowledge. Researchers still lack detailed databases describing the mechanical properties of DNA structures, and simulation tools for predicting behavior at this scale are not yet fully developed.

To overcome these barriers, scientists emphasize the need for collaboration across disciplines. Proposed solutions include creating standardized DNA "parts libraries," using artificial intelligence to improve design and simulation, and advancing bio-manufacturing methods. Progress in these areas will be essential for scaling DNA robots and integrating them into practical applications in healthcare, manufacturing, and beyond.

"The robots of tomorrow won't just be made of metal and plastic," says the research team. "They will be biological, programmable, and intelligent. They will be the tools that allow us to finally master the molecular world."

#10744. AI breakthrough cuts energy use by 100x while boosting accuracy

Artificial intelligence is consuming enormous amounts of electricity in the United States. According to the International Energy Agency, AI systems and data centers used about 415 terawatt hours of power in 2024. That accounts for more than 10% of the country's total electricity production, and demand is projected to double by 2030.

This rapid growth has raised concerns about sustainability. In response, researchers at a School of Engineering have created a proof-of-concept AI system designed to be far more efficient. Their approach could reduce energy use by up to 100 times while also improving performance on tasks.

A Hybrid Approach Called Neuro-Symbolic AI

The research comes from the laboratory of Matthias Scheutz, Karol Family Applied Technology Professor. His team is developing neuro-symbolic AI, which combines traditional neural networks with symbolic reasoning. This method mirrors how people approach problems by breaking them into steps and categories.

The work will be presented at the International Conference of Robotics and Automation in Vienna in May and will appear in the conference proceedings.

Teaching Robots to See, Understand, and Act

Unlike familiar large language models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT and Gemini, the team focuses on AI systems used in robotics. These systems are known as visual-language-action (VLA) models. They extend LLM capabilities by incorporating vision and physical movement.

VLA models take in visual data from cameras and instructions from language, then translate that information into real-world actions. For example, they can control a robot's wheels, arms, or fingers to complete a task.

Why Traditional AI Struggles With Simple Tasks

Conventional VLA systems rely heavily on data and trial-and-error learning. If a robot is asked to stack blocks into a tower, it must first analyze the scene, identify each block, and determine how to place them correctly.

This process often leads to mistakes. Shadows may confuse the system about a block's shape, or the robot may place pieces incorrectly, causing the structure to collapse.

These errors are similar to the problems seen in LLMs. Just as robots can misplace blocks, chatbots can generate false or misleading outputs. Examples include fabricating legal cases or producing images with unrealistic details such as extra fingers.

How Symbolic Reasoning Improves Accuracy and Efficiency

Symbolic reasoning offers a different strategy. Instead of relying only on patterns from data, it uses rules and abstract concepts such as shape and balance. This allows the system to plan more effectively and avoid unnecessary trial and error.

"Like an LLM, VLA models act on statistical results from large training sets of similar scenarios, but that can lead to errors," said Scheutz. "A neuro-symbolic VLA can apply rules that limit the amount of trial and error during learning and get to a solution much faster. Not only does it complete the task much faster, but the time spent on training the system is significantly reduced."

The researchers tested their system using the Tower of Hanoi puzzle, a classic problem that requires careful planning.

The neuro-symbolic VLA achieved a 95% success rate, compared with just 34% for standard systems. When given a more complex version of the puzzle that it had not encountered before, the hybrid system still succeeded 78% of the time. Traditional models failed every attempt.

Training time also dropped sharply. The new system learned the task in only 34 minutes, while conventional models required more than a day and a half.

Massive Energy Savings in Training and Use

Energy consumption was reduced dramatically as well. Training the neuro-symbolic model required only 1% of the energy used by a standard VLA system. During operation, it used just 5% of the energy needed by conventional approaches.

Scheutz compared this inefficiency to everyday AI tools. "These systems are just trying to predict the next word or action in a sequence, but that can be imperfect, and they can come up with inaccurate results or hallucinations. Their energy expense is often disproportionate to the task. For example, when you search on Google, the AI summary at the top of the page consumes up to 100 times more energy than the generation of the website listings."

The Growing Strain of AI on Power Infrastructure

As AI adoption accelerates across industries, demand for computing power continues to climb. Companies are building increasingly large data centers, some of which require hundreds of megawatts of electricity. That level of consumption can exceed the needs of entire small cities.

This trend has sparked a race to expand infrastructure, raising concerns about long-term energy limits.

The researchers suggest that current approaches based on LLMs and VLAs may not be sustainable in the long run. While these systems are powerful, they consume large amounts of energy and can still produce unreliable results.

In contrast, neuro-symbolic AI offers a different direction. By combining learning with structured reasoning, it may provide a more efficient and dependable foundation for future AI systems.

#10743. AI Agents as Insider Threats: Inside Microsoft's Bet on a Unified Security Stack

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

Microsoft's Project Perception adds Guardian Agents to monitor and contain anomalous AI agents, but experts warn that policing unpredictable agents with other agents may compound — not contain — the risk.

Microsoft wants security teams to treat artificial intelligence (AI) agents like they treat employees with privileged access: insiders who can make mistakes, be manipulated, or be compromised.

Earlier this week, the software giant introduced new capabilities to Project Perception, enabling it to discover agents running within an organization, assign an identity and permissions to each agent, and continuously score each organization's risk. When an anomalous agent is discovered in the organization's environment — a problem that Microsoft describes as the "agentic insider" — Project Perception can now cut off the agent's access.

The first release of Project Perception, made available in public preview through Microsoft Defender in August, was designed to defend against AI-driven attacks. Focused on Microsoft's security operations center threat and investigation scenarios, it coordinates red agents to scan for attacker paths, blue agents to identify the greatest risks, and green agents to mitigate threats. Project Perception's initial use was vulnerability management, through MDASH, Microsoft's AI code scanner, which is still in preview. MDASH uses several AI models, including MAI-Cyber-1-Flash, the company's first cybersecurity-specialized model.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

"We're expanding Perception so that we can go secure the AI insider," said Hayete Gallot, executive vice president of Microsoft Security, in a brief video accompanying the announcement.

To do that, Microsoft is adding what it calls Guardian Agents, which monitor the AI-based agents running across an organization and can contain them when they stray into unexpected behavior.

Today, many agents run with the permissions of the user who launched them or by invoking the user's credentials. Microsoft's approach separates the two, Microsoft said in a blog post detailing the new capabilities.

Nadim Abdo, corporate vice president for identity and network access, tells Dark Reading that the system gives every agent a distinct identity separate from the user's "and will ensure that the agent starts with no permissions at all, and only up-scopes to the permissions it needs to complete the task the user is asking it to do,"

Specifically, Microsoft said the new release can detect 35 more types of agents running locally on devices, bringing the total to 60, including Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and GitHub Copilot. It also includes:

Extensions to Microsoft Entra Agent ID that can assign an identity to an agent that was never built to work with Entra.

Dynamic Agent Risk, a continuously updated score built from Entra, Defender, Intune, Purview, Sentinel, and signals from Global Secure Access, Microsoft’s security service edge (SSE) solution that unifies network access and identity protection.

Dynamic Conditional Access for agents, which can block writes while keeping reads, restrict network paths, revoke access, or stop an agent's runtime as risk rises.

Microsoft Execution Container (MXC), a sandbox that keeps credentials and security controls outside the agent's reach.

Related:RemoteThreat Bets Security Teams Need to Test What Happens After Defenses Fail

With Project Perception, Abdo describes an expense-approval agent that reads a malicious instruction hidden in an expense report.

"If someone got a prompt that convinced it to start to try to do wire transfers, we can actually watch it accessing a wire transfer system and say, 'Wait a second, that has nothing to do with the intent,' and that raises its risk," he says.

Microsoft says it can act on rising risk immediately, interrupting an agent's live session, network connection, or runtime without disrupting the user's own work, though those are vendor-stated capabilities in preview.

Project Perception has an expanded agent registry that now shows up across the Microsoft 365 admin center, Defender, Entra, Intune, Purview, and a new Perception Agent Insights view. And Dynamic Agent Risk replaces previously siloed risk scores.

Related:Deception by Design: CISA's Guide to Tricking Cybercriminals

The controls themselves sit outside the agents they watch.

"The first thing [an attacker will] do is they'll manipulate the security controls," Abdo says, so the credentials and monitoring tools run outside the container.

Perception and Agent 365, Microsoft's control plane for governing that was introduced last year and made generally available since May, "need to be battle tested," acknowledged Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella during a fireside chat with Gallot during a CISO conference last week at Microsoft's Redmond, Wash., headquarters. He also admitted that Microsoft's own detection must improve.

"If I look at the state of the art of behavioral monitoring of, let's say, Defender, it has to go way up," he said.

Gallot framed the risk in terms of how models behave.

"Those models have proven to be unpredictable," she said. "They'll do anything they can to get from point A to point B, and what they do may not be what you intend them to do."

Much of what Microsoft describes echoes what other vendors announced in recent weeks. Okta's Agent Gateway separates an agent's permissions from those of the user directing it, and Okta plans a kill switch that would reject tokens already issued to a deactivated agent. Teleport, backed by Cisco, ties privileges to tasks so they disappear when the work ends. CrowdStrike announced an Agentic Identity Provider and Falcon Guardian, which discovers agents and controls that may run on Windows, macOS, and Linux endpoints.

Abdo argues that each vendor sees only part of the picture.

"If you're primarily an identity vendor or primarily a network vendor or primarily an endpoint vendor, that lens gives you some visibility to what agents are doing, but you need to have the other components as well," he says.

Microsoft's advantage, he adds, is that Entra, Defender, and Intune are already widely deployed and integrated, so customers aren't "having to string these things together from multiple vendors."

Microsoft says it will also take in signals from third-party security products. Partners can already publish agent risk events into Agent 365 through public APIs, Abdo says, though he could not yet name which partner integrations are public.

Forrester principal security and risk management analyst Andras Cser is skeptical.

"Most of Microsoft's integration with third-party players, especially in security, has not been first rate so far," Cser says. Because Microsoft has most of the products it needs in its own ecosystem, he adds, it is "interested in pushing its own products."

The question is whether that approach fits environments where agents run across AWS, Google Cloud, Salesforce, and ServiceNow. Last month, Okta announced the formation of the Blueprint Alliance with AWS, CrowdStrike, Google Cloud, Proofpoint, Salesforce, ServiceNow, and Zscaler to develop a shared architecture for securing agents across vendors.

Microsoft is not among the named members. Asked whether it would participate, Abdo said Entra has "always been built on open standards" and that "we're always exploring those things."

Okta, which formed the alliance, argues that no single vendor sees enough.

"No one company can secure agents alone," said CEO and co-founder Todd McKinnon in his keynote at Oktane, the company’s annual conference, last month.

Reacting to this week’s Project Perception launch, Harish Peri, Okta's senior vice president and general manager of AI security, says, "Microsoft's Guardian Agents feature will only be as good as the broader ecosystem it plugs into. If you want to catch intent drift in real time, you need signals pulling from your entire stack, not just one vendor's cloud."

Nevertheless, Peri echoes Nadella's framing. Because agents must be allowed to behave unpredictably to be useful, "we can't secure agents by trying to control how their models think," Peri says. "We need to control their authority."

The answer, Peri says, is "deeper interoperability and cross-vendor signal sharing built on open standards."

Cser interprets the Blueprint Alliance as "more of a partnership kind of map" than a true standard. Cser believes vendor-specific efforts like this alliance are "a marketing ploy" that tend to fade within a year or two. Enterprises need open standards any vendor can implement, he says.

Consequently, that leaves CISOs with an imperfect choice in what Cser calls "still a very fluid market." The current choices, he says, are either a Microsoft-centric approach built mainly on Microsoft products or a multivendor approach with "many vendors, many price lists," where integration "is almost always a suspicious kind of promise."

Some security vendors agree that treating agents as insiders extends the long-standing zero-trust and least-privilege principles rather than replacing them.

Denis Calderone, CTO of Suzu Labs, says the most malicious behavior may never look like an agent straying from its task.

"Dynamic permissions scope what an agent can touch, but the worst outcomes happen inside the authorized envelope," he says.

Calderone points to July's OpenAI incident as evidence that agents can work against the systems watching them. More than 1,000 agents in a cyber evaluation coordinated to game the system grading them, some by faking tool calls, before roughly 700 joined an attack on Hugging Face, according to METR.

Further, Calderone has concerns about Guardian Agents, noting that they are agents themselves.

"Securing agents with agents means the Guardian Agents themselves are overprivileged actors that can be manipulated or compromised," he says.

Cser shares Calderone's concerns about Guardian Agents. An unpredictable agent watched by another unpredictable agent creates "non-deterministic nature squared," Cser says. "Most organizations today are very careful about bringing guardian agents into the mix."

Following Perception's July launch, Forrester principal analyst Allie Mellen urged organizations to enforce "least privilege and least agency," limiting not just what agents can access but what they can do on their own. Microsoft meets the first test but not yet the second, Cser says.

"It is least privilege, but I wouldn't go as far as describing it as least agency," he says, adding that some specialist vendors are further along.

While Perception itself is in public preview, the new Guardian Agent capabilities are in use only inside Microsoft and with "a small set of select customers." They will be expanding to more external customers this week and to broader preview rings over the next few months. Microsoft plans to say more at its annual Ignite conference next month.

Project Perception builds on the controls in Microsoft 365 E7, the $99-per-user-per-month suite that includes E5, Agent 365, and Entra Suite, which supply the signals and enforcement points that Perception relies on. Microsoft hasn't disclosed whether the new capabilities are included in E7, but Project Perception is priced based on consumption.

Cser expects the release to push customers toward E7.

"I would almost be sure that this is another kind of making people buy stuff in more expensive packages that they don't currently need but may need in future," he says.

By his estimate, E7 comes to about $1,200 per user per year at list price, or roughly $600 after typical volume discounts of 40% to 50%, which "can be prohibitively expensive for a lot of organizations."

Meanwhile, Calderone says organizations don't have to wait. He recommends inventorying every agent, including those running on developer machines. Each should be assigned its own identity and credentials set to expire, and each should require human approval for consequential actions.

"That work is free today," he says, "and it's the foundation every one of these Microsoft controls assumes you already have."

Jai Vijayan contributed reporting to this article.

Jeffrey Schwartz is a New York–based freelance writer specializing in information security and enterprise IT. Focused on the constant pace of technological change, Jeff has covered the evolution of technologies, including professional broadcast, computing, networking, the Internet, mobile communications, modern cloud infrastructure and software development for over 30 years.

Jeff has contributed to Dark Reading since 2022 and has written for Channel Futures for over five years. Before launching his freelance career, he was an editor at 1105 Media, where he served as editor-in-chief of Redmond magazine and contributed to its sister publications, including Redmond Channel Partner, Application Development Trends, and Virtualization Review.

Previously, Jeff held editorial roles at CMP Media’s CommunicationsWeek, InternetWeek, and VARBusiness. Earlier contributions include Pro Sound News, Television Broadcast, Videography, Sound & Communications, Post magazine and Crain’s Electronic Media. Jeff holds a Bachelor of Arts degree in Communications and Journalism from Adelphi University. More details are available on Jeff’s LinkedIn profile: https://www.linkedin.com/in/jeffaschwartz.

Most teams set up AI visibility tracking for ChatGPT, add Google, and stop there. Claude tends to come up later, usually when someone notices that half the engineers, analysts and founders they know use it every day. That instinct is sound. Claude's audience leans towards the people who research software and services before they buy.

The numbers back it up. Similarweb put Claude at 3.3% of AI chatbot web visits in February 2026 and 9.2% in May 2026, close to three times the share in three months, while ChatGPT's share kept falling. Those are web visits only. Usage in the Claude apps, in Claude Code and through the API does not show up in that figure, so 9.2% is a floor.

This guide compares six tools that track Claude. Peec AI comes first because it connects Claude answers to the pages behind them. The other five cover different budgets and needs.

A Claude tracking tool sends a fixed set of prompts to Claude on a schedule and records what comes back: whether your brand is named, where in the answer, how it is described, and which sources the answer relied on. Run daily, those records become trends you can compare against competitors.

It is not a rank tracker. Claude gives no list of ten blue links, so the useful numbers are mention rate, position inside the answer, sentiment and cited sources.

How the tool queries Claude. Some tools send your prompts to Anthropic's API. Others drive the Claude app. The two can give different answers, because the app has its own web search behaviour and the API, queried cold, often does not. Neither is wrong. Your buyers use the app, and the API is cheaper to run at scale. What matters is that you know which one you are looking at and that it stays the same over time.

Which plan includes Claude. Claude is a premium engine for several vendors. It can sit on the entry plan, on a higher tier or on Enterprise only, and a free tier often leaves it out.

What it costs per run. Credit-based tools can charge more for Claude than for other engines. Check the credit formula before you size a plan.

Source data. A mention rate says whether Claude names you. Source data says why it does not. Pick a tool that shows the pages Claude read.

Prompt volume. 50 to 150 prompts per brand is a realistic start. Fewer than 15 is mostly noise. Check how many prompts the cheaper tiers cover with Claude specifically: on credit-based tools Claude costs more per run, so the entry plan can cover far fewer Claude prompts than the headline number suggests.

Peec AI is a Berlin-based AI search analytics platform that tracks visibility, position, sentiment and share of voice across AI engines, then shows which sources drive those answers. Claude is part of the Enterprise plan and the agency Scale plan, tracked next to ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Microsoft Copilot and both Google surfaces. That makes it the pick for teams that want Claude as one engine in a wider view rather than as a stand-alone report.

Best for: Teams that track Claude together with ChatGPT and Google and want to know which pages to work on, not only where they stand.

Scrunch AI tracks Claude on its Enterprise plan, alongside nine engines in total. The published Core plan at $250 a month covers four engines and leaves Claude out, so it suits teams that start with ChatGPT, Perplexity, Google and Copilot and add Claude when they move to a quote.

Best for: Teams that want a published entry price now and add Claude through an Enterprise contract later.

Rankscale puts Claude on every paid plan from $99 a month and covers the widest engine list at that price: Claude, Copilot, ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini, both Google surfaces, DeepSeek and Mistral. It is credit-based, and the formula is published, which matters because Claude costs 2 credits per run, more than most engines. On Pro, 1,200 credits cover about 20 prompts run daily on Claude alone.

Best for: Small teams and agencies that want Claude and a long engine list for the least money.

AthenaHQ was built by two engineers who worked on Google Search and DeepMind. Claude is included from the Starter plan, among eleven engines. The free Essential tier does not include Claude, so it shows you the other engines first. Its optimisation agent drafts on-page and off-page recommendations, which suits teams that have the analysis but not the hands to act on it.

Best for: Teams short on people to write the follow-up work.

Profound is the shortest path for companies where an information security review decides the purchase. It lists SOC 2, SSO and SAML on Enterprise and raised a $96M Series C at a $1B valuation in February 2026. Claude is part of the Enterprise engine list, which runs to up to nine engines.

Best for: Enterprises that need a compliance posture on paper before they can buy.

Nightwatch is worth a look if you want Claude mentions next to the keyword rankings you already track and you are not paying for one of the large SEO suites. AI tracking is included in the plan price.

Best for: SEO teams that want one dashboard for classic rankings and Claude.

If Claude is one engine among several and you need to know what to fix, choose the tool with source analysis. If Claude is the only new engine and budget decides, Rankscale and Nightwatch cost the least. If you have a security review to pass, start with Profound or Peec AI's Enterprise plan. If you have no Claude coverage at all and cannot add a vendor, a few tools let you connect your own Anthropic API key, and Anthropic then bills you directly for the runs.

Claude is now a real share of the AI answers your buyers read, and its answers often differ from ChatGPT's. A single-engine number gives you false confidence in either direction. Peec AI is the strongest choice for teams that want Claude as part of a full view of sources, gaps and actions, with the caveat that Claude requires the Enterprise plan or, for agencies, the Scale plan. For the cheapest route to Claude coverage, Rankscale and Nightwatch are the practical options, though Rankscale's entry plan covers only about 20 daily Claude prompts, against 50 AI prompts on Nightwatch's entry plan. Whichever you choose, ask how the tool queries Claude and keep that method fixed. A tool measures. What moves the number is being on the pages Claude reads, and the best Claude tracking tools show you which ones those are.

Does Claude cite the same sources as ChatGPT?

Often not, and that is the practical reason to track it. Being named in one engine tells you little about the other.

How do I turn Claude tracking results into something I can act on?

Look for source data, not only a mention rate. A mention rate says whether Claude names you, while source data shows which pages Claude relied on and where competitors are cited and you are not. Peec AI classifies every cited page, reports the gaps and ranks recommended actions from them, and AthenaHQ goes a step further by drafting follow-up content. #10740. Thieves steal 5,000 endangered ants from nature reserve in bizarre theft

Thieves have stolen an entire colony of rare ants from a protected nature reserve, with as many as 5,000 insects potentially taken.

The colony of narrow-headed ants was removed from the reserve in Devon, England, the species’ “last stronghold” in the country.

The theft was discovered during routine checks in mid-October, when researchers found a hole where one of the nests had previously been.

According to Devon Wildlife Trust, the ground around the missing nest showed signs of digging with a spade, suggesting someone had deliberately removed the colony.

A single narrow-headed ant nest can contain between 1,000 and 5,000 ants, including breeding queens that can live for up to 25 years. However, the exact number taken remains unknown.

The species was once much more widespread across England, but habitat loss has reduced its population to a single remaining location. Small numbers also survive in Scotland.

Julia Balfour, a species recovery officer at Devon Wildlife Trust, explained that the loss of even one colony could have lasting consequences.

“The removal of an established nest is a significant loss for this species. Narrow-headed Ant colonies develop slowly, and each mature nest, with its long-lived queens, represents many years of growth that cannot quickly be replaced,” she said.

“Our most recent survey recorded 142 active nests on the nature reserve, so every nest matters. This is the last population of Narrow-headed Ants in England, and losing even one colony sets back years of careful work by our staff, volunteers and partners.”

#10739. This new chip survives 1300°F (700°C) and could change AI forever

Modern electronics power everything from smartphones to satellites, but they all share a major limitation. Heat. Once temperatures climb above roughly 200 degrees Celsius, most devices begin to break down. For decades, this thermal barrier has been one of the toughest challenges in engineering.

Researchers at the University of Southern California now believe they have found a way past that limit.

In a study published on March 26, 2026 in Science, a team led by Joshua Yang, Arthur B. Freeman Chair Professor at the Ming Hsieh Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the USC Viterbi School of Engineering and the USC School of Advanced Computing, unveiled a new type of memory device that continues to operate at 700 degrees Celsius (~1300 degrees Fahrenheit). That temperature exceeds molten lava and goes far beyond anything previously achieved for this class of technology. The device showed no sign of failure. In fact, 700 degrees was simply the maximum their equipment could test.

"You may call it a revolution," Yang said. "It is the best high-temperature memory ever demonstrated."

The new device is known as a memristor, a nanoscale component that can both store data and perform computations. It is constructed like a microscopic layered structure, with two electrodes on either side and a thin ceramic layer in between.

Jian Zhao, the study's first author, built the device using tungsten for the top electrode, hafnium oxide ceramic in the middle, and graphene for the bottom layer. Tungsten has the highest melting point of any element, while graphene, a single-atom-thick sheet of carbon, is known for its exceptional strength and heat resistance.

This combination produced remarkable performance. The device retained data for more than 50 hours at 700 degrees without needing to be refreshed. It also endured over one billion switching cycles at that temperature and operated at just 1.5 volts with speeds measured in tens of nanoseconds.

The discovery was not part of the team's original plan. They were initially attempting to create a different graphene-based device, which did not work as intended. Along the way, they encountered something surprising.

"To be honest, it was by accident, as most discoveries are," Yang said. "If you can predict it, it's usually not surprising, and probably not significant enough."

Further investigation revealed why the device performed so well. In conventional electronics, heat causes metal atoms in the top electrode to slowly migrate through the ceramic layer. Eventually, they reach the bottom electrode, creating a permanent connection that short-circuits the device and leaves it stuck in the on state.

Graphene prevents this failure. Its interaction with tungsten is, as Yang described it, similar to oil and water. Tungsten atoms that approach the graphene surface cannot attach to it. Without a stable point to settle, they drift away instead of forming a conductive bridge. This prevents short circuits and preserves the device's function even under extreme heat.

The researchers confirmed this mechanism using advanced electron microscopy, spectroscopy, and quantum-level simulations. By understanding what happens at the atomic interface, they have turned an unexpected result into a principle that could guide future designs. Other materials with similar surface properties could be identified, which may help scale the technology for industrial production.

Electronics capable of operating above 500 degrees Celsius have long been a goal for space exploration. Venus, for example, has a surface temperature around that level, and every lander sent there has failed in part due to extreme heat. Current silicon-based chips cannot survive such conditions.

"We are now above 700 degrees, and we suspect it will go higher," Yang said.

The potential applications go far beyond space missions. Geothermal energy systems require electronics that can function deep underground, where surrounding rock can glow red-hot. Nuclear and fusion systems also expose equipment to intense heat. Even in everyday settings, durability improves significantly. A device rated for 700 degrees would be extremely robust at the roughly 125-degree temperatures often reached inside automotive electronics.

Why It Matters for Artificial Intelligence

In addition to storing data, the device offers a major advantage for artificial intelligence. Many AI systems rely heavily on matrix multiplication, a mathematical operation used in tasks like image recognition and language processing. Traditional computers perform these calculations step by step, consuming large amounts of energy.

Memristors approach the problem differently. By using Ohm's Law, where voltage times conductance equals current, the device performs calculations directly as electricity flows through it. The result is obtained instantly as the measured current.

"Over 92 percent of the computing in AI systems like ChatGPT is nothing but matrix multiplication," Yang said. "This type of device can perform that in the most efficient way, orders of magnitude faster and at lower energy."

Yang and three co-authors of the study (Qiangfei Xia, Miao Hu, and Ning Ge) have already co-founded a company called TetraMem to commercialize memristor-based AI chips at room temperature. Their lab is already using working chips from TetraMem for machine learning tasks. The high-temperature version described in this research could extend those capabilities to environments where traditional electronics cannot operate, allowing devices such as spacecraft or industrial sensors to process data directly on site.

From Lab Prototype to Real-World Technology

Despite the promising results, Yang emphasizes that practical applications are still some distance away. Memory is only one part of a complete computing system. High-temperature logic circuits will also need to be developed and integrated. In addition, the current devices were built manually at very small scales in a laboratory setting, so manufacturing at scale will take time.

"This is the first step," Yang said. "It's still a long way to go. But logically, you can see: now it makes it possible. The missing component has been made."

From a manufacturing perspective, two of the materials used in the device, tungsten and hafnium oxide, are already widely used in semiconductor production. Graphene is newer but is actively being developed by major companies such as TSMC and Samsung, and it has already been produced at wafer scale in research environments.

The work was conducted through the CONCRETE Center, short for Center of Neuromorphic Computing under Extreme Environments, a multi-university Center of Excellence led by USC and supported by the Air Force Office of Scientific Research and the Air Force Research Laboratory. Key experimental work was carried out in collaboration with Dr. Sabyasachi Ganguli's team at the AFRL Materials Lab in Dayton, Ohio, while theoretical analysis involved USC researchers and collaborators at Kumamoto University in Japan.

For Yang, publication in Science reflects more than a single achievement.

"Space exploration has never been so real, so close, and at such a large scale," he said. "This paper represents a critical leap into a much larger, more exciting frontier."

#10737. This new chip could slash data center energy waste

As data centers consume more energy to support growing digital demands, engineers at the University of California San Diego have introduced a new chip design that could make powering graphics processing units (GPUs) more efficient. The innovation focuses on a key function in electronics: converting high voltages into the lower levels required by computing hardware. In laboratory testing, a prototype chip successfully performed this type of voltage conversion with high efficiency under conditions similar to those found in modern data centers.

The findings, published in Nature Communications, suggest the potential for smaller and more energy-efficient systems in advanced computing environments.

Rethinking DC-DC Converters for Modern Electronics

At the center of the new design is an improved version of a widely used component known as a DC-DC step-down converter. These converters are found in nearly all electronic devices and serve as a critical link between power sources and sensitive circuits. Their job is to take a high incoming voltage and reduce it to the exact level needed for safe operation.

In data centers, electricity is often distributed at 48 volts, while GPU processors typically require much lower voltages, usually between 1 and 5 volts. Efficiently managing this large voltage drop has become increasingly challenging as computing systems grow more powerful and compact.

Limits of Traditional Power Conversion Technology

Conventional step-down converters often struggle when dealing with large differences between input and output voltage. As that gap increases, efficiency drops and it becomes harder to supply enough current. Most existing designs rely on magnetic components such as inductors. While these components have been refined over many years, they are approaching their practical limits and are becoming harder to improve further.

"We've gotten so good at designing inductive converters that there's not really much room left to improve them to meet future needs," said study senior author Patrick Mercier, professor in the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the UC San Diego Jacobs School of Engineering.

Exploring Piezoelectric Resonators as an Alternative

To move beyond these limitations, Mercier and his team, including first author Jae-Young Ko, an electrical and computer engineering Ph.D. student at UC San Diego, investigated a different approach using piezoelectric resonators. These small devices store and transfer energy through mechanical vibrations rather than magnetic fields.

Converters based on piezoelectric components could offer several advantages. They have the potential to be smaller, more energy dense, more efficient, and easier to manufacture at scale. "They have a lot of room to grow and have the potential to deliver better performance than anything that's come before them," Mercier said.

However, earlier versions of piezoelectric converters have had difficulty maintaining efficiency and delivering sufficient power when handling large voltage differences.

Hybrid Design Achieves High Efficiency and Power Output

To overcome these issues, the researchers created a hybrid converter that combines a piezoelectric resonator with small, commercially available capacitors arranged in a carefully designed configuration. This setup enables the system to handle larger voltage conversions more effectively.

The team incorporated this design into a prototype chip and tested its performance. The device successfully converted 48 volts down to 4.8 volts -- a level commonly required in data centers -- with a peak efficiency of 96.2 percent. It also delivered roughly four times more output current than previous piezoelectric-based designs.

This hybrid approach offers several benefits. It creates multiple pathways for energy to move through the system, reduces wasted power, and lessens the strain on the resonator. Together, these improvements enhance both efficiency and power delivery while only slightly increasing the chip's size.

Challenges and Next Steps for Real-World Use

Although the technology shows strong promise, it is still in the early stages of development. The researchers view it as an important step toward overcoming the constraints of current power conversion systems. Future efforts will focus on refining materials, improving circuit designs, and developing better packaging methods.

One challenge is that piezoelectric resonators physically vibrate, which means they cannot be attached to circuit boards using standard soldering techniques. New integration strategies will be needed to incorporate them into electronic systems, Mercier explained.

"Piezoelectric-based converters aren't quite ready to replace existing power converter technologies yet," Mercier added. "But they offer a trajectory for improvement. We need to continue to improve on multiple areas -- materials, circuits and packaging -- to make this technology ready for data center applications."

This project was supported in part by the Power Management Integration Center (PMIC), an Industry-University Cooperative Research Center (IUCRC) funded by the National Science Foundation (award number 2052809).

#10736. Publisher blames “AI-slop” on Steam as their game only gets 15 players at launch

An indie game publisher has slammed Steam after its new release attracted just 15 players despite receiving more than 11,000 wishlists, blaming a flood of AI-generated games for disrupting its launch.

Steam has become increasingly crowded in recent years, with thousands of games arriving on Valve’s PC storefront every month. As the use of generative AI becomes more widespread, some developers are concerned about how it’s affecting smaller studios.

Now, publisher 2 Left Thumbs has accused Steam’s approval process of damaging the release of its new co-op game, Wheel Make It.

Developed by tlproductions, Wheel Make It is a physics-based game where two players control the wheels of a single wheelchair, working together to navigate obstacles. It was originally scheduled to launch on October 12, but problems during Steam’s review process prevented it from releasing on time.

According to the developers’ October 12 announcement, the game had already been awaiting approval for around two weeks. This was because reviewers encountered difficulties accessing its local co-op mode, although the publisher says “you literally just share a keyboard.”

Further complications followed, with the game eventually launching on November 1. However, despite accumulating more than 11,000 wishlists, it peaked at just 15 concurrent players in the 24 hours after release.

We were assured by Steam that missing our launch – as a result of the tidal wave of AI-slop that destroyed their review queue – would not affect the usual mechanisms of launch visibilityI beg to differ…11,000+ wishlists and this is what our launch turned into https://t.co/ss75LSraHg pic.twitter.com/t7gR2yFj8x

“We were assured by Steam that missing our launch – as a result of the tidal wave of AI-slop that destroyed their review queue – would not affect the usual mechanisms of launch visibility,” the publisher wrote in an X post.

“I beg to differ… 11,000+ wishlists and this is what our launch turned into.”

The complaint comes amid a sharp increase in AI-generated content on Steam. As Dexerto previously reported, an analysis of approximately 63,600 releases found that 49.9% of games launched in October 2026 disclosed using AI, compared with just 1.7% in January 2024.

However, those figures don’t establish that AI-generated games caused the delays experienced by Wheel Make It. While the publisher believes the disrupted release damaged its visibility, Valve has not publicly confirmed that AI submissions were responsible for the review backlog.

#10734. 8 Checks Developers Should Add Before Importing PDF Tables into an Application

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A PDF table can look correct and still produce unreliable application data. A wrapped description becomes two rows. An account code loses its leading zeros. A repeated page header is imported as a transaction. A missing decimal separator changes an amount without triggering an obvious error.

These problems are easy to overlook when an exported spreadsheet opens successfully. But opening a workbook proves very little about whether its contents belong in a database.

For developers building reporting dashboards, inventory systems, or document-import features, PDF extraction should feed a validation workflow. The following eight checks help separate readable output from data your application can safely process.

The examples use fictional invoice-style records and Python. They demonstrate a narrow validation contract rather than a complete PDF conversion service.

Not all PDFs contain the same kind of information.

A digitally generated document may include selectable text and vector lines. A scanned document may contain only page images. A mixed document can contain both, sometimes with an existing OCR layer that is incomplete or inaccurate.

Inspect representative pages before committing to an extraction strategy. Check whether text is selectable, whether copied Check parsing and validation behavior against fixtures

The pdfplumber documentation explains its text and table capabilities, including visual debugging. Its strengths are primarily associated with machine-generated PDFs; it is not an OCR engine.

OCRmyPDF adds a searchable text layer to scans. That does not, by itself, reconstruct a correct table schema. You still need to determine which text belongs in each row and column.

Practical check: Build a sample set containing a clean digital PDF, a scan, and a multi-page table before evaluating the extraction path.

A conversion step should create an inspectable intermediate result. It should not automatically authorize database writes.

For workflows that need a spreadsheet as the intermediate format, Lido is one option for converting PDF content to Excel. Evaluate the output against representative documents, then apply the same schema and reconciliation checks you would use with a custom extraction script.

Commit accepted records to the application.

This structure lets you replace an extraction tool without changing every downstream rule. It also provides a place to inspect failures before they become production records.

SitePoint’s guide to parsing spreadsheet data with Python provides background on working with spreadsheet formats in an application workflow.

Practical check: The importer should be able to reject a workbook even when conversion completed successfully.

Column names alone are not a sufficient contract. A field called “Date” could represent an invoice date, payment date, or service date.

Decide how repeated headers, subtotal rows, footnotes, and blank lines will be identified. Do not let them disappear through undocumented cleanup rules.

Load a workbook with deliberate type handling

The pandas read_excel reference documents these loading options. Using strings limits unwanted interpretation at this stage, while keep_default_na=False preserves values that would otherwise match default missing-value markers.

However, reading a cell as text cannot recover information already lost upstream. If a converter stored 00127 as the number 127, this setting will not reconstruct the original ID.

Practical check: Compare identifiers against the original document, including examples with leading zeros.

Removing every comma and currency symbol may look convenient, but it hides ambiguity. The strings follow different conventions.

Choose an explicit format per document family. The following parser accepts a deliberately narrow format: ASCII digits, optional correctly grouped thousands commas, a decimal point, and up to two decimal places. It permits a leading minus sign for adjustments.

This intentionally rejects parentheses, currency symbols, exponent notation, and comma-decimal formatting. Those formats may be valid in other documents, but supporting them requires an explicit rule.

Python’s Decimal documentation explains decimal arithmetic. Constructing a Decimal directly from the validated string avoids first introducing a binary floating-point representation.

Practical check: Keep the original extracted value alongside the normalized value, and reconcile the result against other evidence.

A hundred extracted rows are not necessarily the correct hundred rows. One line may be missing while another is duplicated.

Required fields are present and nonempty.

Dates are valid under the declared format.

Line identifiers are unique within the correct scope.

Recognized line-item totals reconcile with the appropriate subtotal.

Each accepted row has a traceable source location.

For a document whose stated subtotal is exactly the sum of its line amounts:

Do not compare that subtotal directly with a grand total containing tax, shipping, or other adjustments. First model those components.

Avoid a generic tolerance such as “accept differences below one dollar.” If the document requires rounding, define where rounding occurs, the currency precision, and the permitted discrepancy.

SitePoint’s overview of data preprocessing provides additional context for separating cleaning, transformation, and integration.

Practical check: Inject one missing row and one duplicate into your fixtures. Confirm that the workflow detects both.

When a record fails validation, a reviewer should not have to search a long PDF without context.

Keep a reference to the source document, page number, extraction run, and original field value. Where the extractor exposes cell coordinates, retain them so a review interface can highlight the relevant region.

Distinguish “not extracted,” “blank in source,” and “not applicable.” Turning all three into an empty string makes it harder to understand what happened.

Confidence scores can help prioritize work, but they are not interchangeable across tools and do not replace business validation. A highly confident extraction can still be placed in the wrong column.

Practical check: Ask someone unfamiliar with the document to resolve a flagged record using only the review interface and its source reference.

An import may stop after extraction, during validation, or while writing records. Retrying should not create another copy of every accepted line.

Assign each import a stable identity. A document hash can help identify byte-identical uploads, while an explicit tenant or account scope prevents unrelated users’ imports from being treated as one.

A hash alone is insufficient for every duplicate policy. Two differently encoded PDFs may represent the same invoice, and one file may legitimately need reprocessing after a parser correction.

Track both the document identity and processing version. Separate extraction attempts from committed business records.

At the database boundary, define the appropriate uniqueness rule and use a transaction for the unit you promise to import atomically. For example, invoice lines might be unique by account, invoice identity, and line number—not by invoice ID alone across all customers.

When reprocessing changes existing values, make that an explicit replacement or correction workflow rather than an unnoticed side effect of retrying.

Practical check: Run the same accepted import twice and verify that the application record count remains unchanged.

The most valuable fixtures are not always the most visually complicated. A tiny change can alter business meaning while producing valid-looking data.

Use pytest parameterization to exercise numeric-format boundarie. SitePoint’s Python unit-testing guide explains the broader testing workflow.

Parser tests do not verify the extraction engine. Add end-to-end fixtures with manually verified expected records for repeated headers, wrapped descriptions, scans, and multi-page tables.

Measure field accuracy and the number of documents that pass all required checks. A strong average can conceal a weak result on the one field your application depends on most.

Practical check: Retain a regression fixture for every meaningful production failure, using synthetic or appropriately sanitized documents.

PDF conversion produces candidate data. Your application decides whether that data is complete, consistent, and suitable for use.

A dependable workflow identifies the source format, preserves extraction evidence, enforces explicit column rules, reconciles values, and makes retries predictable.

Start with one document family and a small verified fixture set. Expand only when you can explain both why a record was accepted and how a reviewer can investigate one that was rejected.

#10733. “Giant superatoms” could finally solve quantum computing’s biggest problem

Researchers at Chalmers University of Technology in Sweden have introduced a new theoretical design for quantum systems based on what they call "giant superatoms." This concept offers a fresh way to protect, control, and share quantum information, potentially bringing scientists closer to building large-scale quantum computers.

Quantum computers are expected to transform fields like drug discovery and encryption by solving problems that are far beyond the reach of conventional machines. However, progress has been limited by a major challenge known as decoherence. This occurs when quantum bits, or qubits, lose their information due to interactions with their surroundings. Even small amounts of electromagnetic noise can disrupt the fragile quantum states needed for computation.

"Quantum systems are extraordinarily powerful but also extremely fragile. The key to making them useful is learning how to control their interaction with the surrounding environment," says Lei Du, postdoctoral researcher in applied quantum technology at Chalmers.

Lei Du is the lead author of a study that outlines this new type of quantum system. The design is built around giant superatoms, which combine several important features. These systems reduce decoherence, remain stable, and consist of multiple interconnected "atoms" that function together as a single unit.

Giant superatoms bring together two previously separate ideas in quantum physics: giant atoms and superatoms. While each has been studied on its own, this is the first time they have been merged into a single system. These structures behave like atoms but are not found in nature. Instead, they are engineered by scientists (see fact box below).

The idea of giant atoms was first introduced by researchers at Chalmers over a decade ago and is now widely used in the field. A giant atom is typically designed as a qubit (which is the smallest unit of quantum information). Unlike ordinary atoms, it connects to light or sound waves at multiple, physically separated points. This allows it to interact with its environment in several places at once, helping it preserve quantum information.

"Waves that leave one connection point can travel through the environment and return to affect the atom at another point -- similar to hearing an echo of your own voice before you've finished speaking. This self-interaction leads to highly beneficial quantum effects, reduces decoherence and gives the system a form of memory of past interactions," explains Anton Frisk Kockum, Associate Professor of Applied Quantum Physics at Chalmers and co-author of the study.

Although giant atoms have improved understanding of quantum behavior, they have had limitations when it comes to entanglement. Entanglement allows multiple qubits to share a single quantum state and act as one coordinated system, which is essential for powerful quantum computers.

To overcome this limitation, the research team combined giant atoms with the concept of superatoms. A superatom consists of several natural atoms that share the same quantum state and behave collectively as one larger atom.

This combination is expected to make it easier to create complex quantum states needed for quantum communication, networks, and highly sensitive measurement systems.

"A giant superatom may be envisaged as multiple giant atoms working together as a single entity, exhibiting a non-local interaction between light and matter. This enables quantum information from multiple qubits to be stored and controlled within one unit, without the need for increasingly complex surrounding circuitry," explains Lei Du.

"Giant superatoms open the door to entirely new capabilities, giving us a powerful new toolbox. They allow us to control quantum information and create entanglement in ways that were previously extremely difficult, or even impossible," says Janine Splettstoesser, Professor of Applied Quantum Physics at Chalmers and co-author of the study.

Toward Scalable and Practical Quantum Systems

This work creates new possibilities for building quantum systems that are both scalable and reliable. The researchers plan to move from theory toward actually constructing these systems. Their design could also be integrated with other quantum technologies, serving as a building block for connecting different types of quantum platforms.

"There is currently strong interest in hybrid approaches, in which different quantum systems work together, because each has its own strengths," says Anton Frisk Kockum. "Our research shows that smart design can reduce the need for increasingly complex hardware and giant superatoms are bringing us one step closer to practically applicable quantum technology."

More on: Methods for protecting, controlling and distributing quantum information

The study shows that the way giant superatoms interact with light depends on their internal quantum states. This discovery gives researchers greater control over how quantum information moves through a system. They describe two different ways of connecting these structures to achieve useful outcomes.

In one setup, several giant superatoms are closely linked in a specific arrangement. This allows them to pass quantum states between each other without decoherence, meaning no information is lost.

In another setup, the atoms are spaced farther apart but connected in a carefully tuned way so that waves remain synchronized. This makes it possible to direct quantum signals and distribute entanglement over long distances.

Superatoms and giant atoms are engineered systems that behave like atoms rather than naturally occurring ones.

A superatom is a quantum system made up of multiple natural atoms that share a single quantum state and respond to light as one entity.

A giant atom, on the other hand, connects to light or sound waves at several separate points in space. It is called "giant" because it is larger than the wavelength of the light it interacts with.

Giant atoms have defined energy levels and follow the rules of quantum mechanics, yet they can reach sizes of up to millimeters, making them visible to the naked eye. Through electromagnetic or acoustic waves, they can interact with their surroundings at multiple locations at the same time. One way to picture this is as a single atom linked to a wave at several distant points. This unusual setup allows the atom to be influenced by the waves it produces.

A man in Japan returned a $300,000 rare watch with an apology letter after stealing it from a store.

For most thieves, the aim of the game is to steal something and get away with it. They never typically aim to get caught or even have to hand the items back.

However, over in Japan, one man decided to issue an apology after he snatched a rare Audemars Piguet watch worth around $292,000. As per The Japan Times, the robbery happened on October 29 in Tokyo’s Nakano Ward.

The man, who hasn’t been named, asked to try on the rare watch before fleeing the store and escaping the two employees who were working at the time.

On November 1, he returned the watch via a courier and left a note saying sorry for the robbery, with the returned watch as well.

The store confirmed that it was the watch that had been stolen, as they checked the serial number.

While the apology note did contain a name and address on it, employees believe the details are fake. An investigation is still ongoing, with CCTV footage of the man seemingly spotting him travelling via train and taxi during his getaway.
